transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-21 11:00 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Priya, Tom, Ellen, Raj (Skyforge)

Summary: Quick econ scrub of pilot. Focus on where caching bought us savings, what batching we've tried, and next runs.

[00:00] Samir (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we've got about 40 minutes. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Priya (Customer): Priya here, ML eng, hi.
[00:10] Tom (Customer): Tom from infra, hi.
[00:12] Ellen (Customer): Ellen, product.
[00:14] Raj (Customer): Raj, CTO.
[00:17] Samir: Cool. Maya and I will run through the recent numbers then dig into caching and batching tradeoffs.
[00:23] Maya (SE): I pulled the last week's pilot runs — we saw nominal throughput at about 1.6k tokens/sec per GPU for the base gen-7-small variant with default batching at 64, burst enabled. That maps to roughly 0.0038 dollars per 1k tokens, when you normalize for GPU uptime and token length distribution.
[01:05] Priya: Sorry, can you repeat tokens/sec? Our front load has a lot of short prompts so our average token length is lower.
[01:12] Maya: Yeah — 1,600 tokens per second per GPU on the sample trace we used. But note that's with a 1.2k median response length; if your prompts average 200 tokens the effective tokens/sec/$ will look better.
[01:33] Tom: Where are you seeing biggest cost wins? Was it batching or the caching?
[01:38] Maya: The largest single delta came from prefix/KV caching for repeated system prompts. When we enabled KV cache with a 4k prefix retention window we saw about a 22% token-cost reduction because cached KV entries avoided re-computing attention for the prefix. Batching added ~18% throughput improvement but at a slightly higher p50 latency — about +30 to 50ms.
[02:10] Samir: To be clear, caching saved token work on the KV side, batching saved kernel amortization. So they stack, but there's diminishing returns. With both on we measured about 35% unit cost reduction vs baseline.
[02:28] Ellen: That 35% is promising — can you explain the assumptions in that calc? We want to present to finance.
[02:34] Maya: Sure. Baseline = gen-7-small at batch 1, no caching, median tokens 1.2k. Baseline token compute cost measured as GPU cycles over run. We then applied measured throughput gains from batching and reduced compute from cached prefixes. The workbook Samir will send breaks this down by model variant and percentiles.
[03:01] Priya: We also worry about tail latency for our interactive flows. If batching helps throughput but adds p95 spikes, that's a problem.
[03:09] Maya: Absolutely — in our traces p50 increased slightly with larger batch sizes, p95 increased more. For example at batch 128 p50 was +45ms, p95 +200ms. But you can use dynamic batching windows and latency SLO cutoffs to cap that. Redwood's routing supports a latency-first policy to keep interactive traffic on low-batch lanes.
[03:38] Raj: Any difference if we switch to a quantized variant? We tried a int4 version in our staging but saw quality drop.
[03:46] Maya: Quantization typically reduces cost by another 12–25% depending on model and runtime kernels. But as you said quality can drop. We recommend running a small eval set (5–10% of production prompts) to measure perplexity and downstream metrics. The Optimize suggestions will rank quant profiles by quality loss.
[04:10] Tom: VPC and data residency stuff — we need to validate logs and KMS integration before we can push more traffic.
[04:17] Samir: Understood. We can provision a private pilot (VPC peering + customer-managed KMS) — that gives you no data path through public endpoints and lets keys stay in your HSM. We do need the peering info and a security contact.
[04:32] Tom: I'll open the peering ticket after this call. We'll also need a short security questionnaire answered for SOC2 artifacts.
[04:38] Samir: Great — will set that up with our security team.
[04:42] Priya: Quick follow on on caching: how often do you evict prefixes? We have many long-lived sessions where the same system prompt appears.
[04:52] Maya: Eviction is LRU with size-based windows. For pilot we configured a 4k token window and TTL of 48 hours. That captured most of your repeated sessions. If you have very long-lived sessions we can bump the window or store client-side short-lived session ids to boost hit rate. Hit rate in your workload was about 42% during peak.
[05:18] Ellen: 42% hit rate — how much headroom do we have to improve that?
[05:22] Maya: Several levers: increase the window, tune the prefix extraction logic to include more of the repeated system prompts, or move static context to a static embedding store. Each has tradeoffs for memory and KV usage. For example doubling window to 8k gained another ~9% hit rate in our microbenchmarks but increased memory by ~2x.
[05:46] Priya: About batching: are there runtime knobs we can adjust dynamically? We have spikes of traffic during sync jobs.
[05:53] Maya: Yes — Redwood supports per-route batching profiles and dynamic burst capacity. You can set a small low-latency lane for interactive routes and a high-throughput lane for batch jobs. The router will auto-fallback if capacity limits hit.
[06:10] Samir: Also, note our autoscaler supports priority tiers so if you want dedicated capacity for high-QPS windows we can set reserved nodes. That reduces preemption risk and smooths tokens/sec.
[06:22] Raj: Pricing model question — the tokens/sec/$ calc you mentioned includes GPU amortized cost only? Or network/infra?
[06:30] Maya: The spreadsheet includes GPU instance cost, storage for KV, and an overhead allowance for control-plane. It doesn't include your internal network costs for VPC egress; we call that out separately. We'll label each line item so finance can reconcile.
[06:48] Tom: Any suggestions for initial pilot config to optimize unit cost without sacrificing latency?
[06:53] Maya: Start with: 1) Keep interactive routes on batch size 8–16, latency-first policy; 2) Enable KV prefix caching with 4k window and monitor hit rate; 3) Use moderate quantization candidate (int8) for low-risk back-end flows; 4) Run a 1-hour stress benchmark with these settings and with caching off as control. Maya will run that.
[07:20] Priya: For evaluation we'll need a scoring set. I can deliver a 500 prompt subset representative of production.
[07:26] Priya: Side note — occasionally we saw weird tokenization differences when switching model variants. Could that change cost numbers?
[07:33] Maya: Yes, tokenization and model vocabulary differences can change token counts meaningfully. We'll normalize by running our scripts on your prompt set and including tokens-per-prompt in the workbook.
[07:46] Ellen: How do rollouts work if we want canary a quantized variant?
[07:50] Samir: Redwood rollouts let you route percentage traffic to a variant and automatically fallback on quality regressions. You can tie rollouts to eval sets and abort if metrics drop. We'll send the rollout runbook.
[08:05] Raj: Competitors — we did a quick spike with Anthropic and saw marginally lower latency but higher $/token. Do you have any benchmarking guidance to make apples-to-apples compares?
[08:15] Maya: Yes — run same prompt set, same target latency tiers, and report p50/p95 and tokens-per-response. Also confirm model families and quantization parity. We'll help map equivalent model capacity.
[08:30] Tom: For the benchmark Maya will need SSH to a bastion? Is that how you collect low-level perf?
[08:35] Maya: For private pilots yes, we collect GPU logs through an agent. For hosted we can provide aggregated perf metrics. For your private pilot we'll ask for a short-lived access account for the benchmark window.
[08:48] Priya: On initial runs we noticed occasional hallucination regressions with quantized variants. We'll include those prompts in the eval set.
[08:55] Maya: Good plan — include top 50 failure prompts. The Optimize tooling will surface regressions and suggest different quant levels or fallback policies.
[09:05] Samir: Anything else from Skyforge?
[09:07] Priya: Timeline: we'd like to decide on Dedicated vs Hosted after these runs by end of month.
[09:12] Raj: Agreed — finance wants a clear tokens/sec/$ delta.
[09:16] Samir: Ok we'll prioritize the cost workbook and the KV-bench. I'll send the cost workbook today, Maya runs the bench tomorrow, Tom opens infra tickets. We'll reconvene next Friday same time.
[09:28] Ellen: Sounds good.
[09:30] Tom: Quick Q — is there a simple toggle to force cache bypass for debugging?
[09:33] Maya: Yes — you can set ?cache=off on requests or route-level override. We'll include examples in the config doc.
[09:40] Samir: Great. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with the documents and the meeting notes.
[09:45] Priya: Thanks.
[09:46] Raj: Thanks all.

End of transcript.

Referenced artifacts/links: cost workbook (link: drive.redwood/costs/skyforge-redacted.xlsx), pilot benchmark logs (to be uploaded to shared s3/bucket), rollout runbook (docs.redwood/rollouts), security questionnaire (docs.redwood/security/sq-skyforge.pdf)
